summary: The People could withdraw consent to a resentencing that omitted postrelease supervision. The order was affirmed.
Search incident to arrest produced narcotics evidence. Suppression analysis turned on lawful custodial arrest and contemporaneous search authority.
Appeal did not present the legal issue framed by defendant. No reviewable question warranting relief.
Modified severance satisfied governing severance standards. No showing of substantial prejudice from joint proceedings as limited by the trial court.
Proof failed to satisfy the governing statutory standard in both matters. Supreme Court improperly assessed defendants under an incorrect legal threshold.
Defendant, facing multiple felony charges, pleaded guilty to one count of robbery in the first degree. The order was affirmed, in a memorandum.
The consecutive character of a new sentence is a collateral, not direct, plea consequence. The plea allocution was therefore not defective on that ground.
Any evidentiary error was harmless given overwhelming proof of guilt. No reasonable possibility that the challenged rulings affected the verdict.
Defendant's trial counsel was not ineffective for failing to object under CPL 710.30 to testimony about a victim's out-of-court identification. The order was affirmed.
Routine breathalyzer calibration and maintenance records were nontestimonial and not barred by Crawford. The order was affirmed.
Corroboration challenge under CPL 60.50 failed on this record. Independent evidence sufficiently supported the reliability of the statement.
DLRA relief construed in light of the statute's ameliorative purpose. Rockefeller Drug Law resentencing principles applied as limited by statutory text.
No preserved claim warranted reversal under the governing standards. The order was affirmed.
Counsel was ineffective for overlooking a dispositive issue on this record. The order was reversed and a new trial ordered.
Warrant scope challenge failed. Search and seizure remained within authorized parameters.
Preclusion of defense testimony constituted error. Materiality assessment supported potential verdict significance.
Expert testimony was insufficiently cabined and hypothetical questioning improperly bolstered identity proof. Evidentiary limits on expert proof were violated.
Spoliation finding supported an adverse-inference charge regarding destroyed video evidence. Preservation request predated destruction.
Assumed testimonial notices were admitted in error. Error harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.
Preservation is required because the mode of proceedings exception is not applicable to such a claim. The order was affirmed.
Appearance-of-impropriety concerns required strict neutrality safeguards. Public confidence and defendant fairness interests controlled.
Record supported tax-related and financial-fraud elements charged. Required federal and state tax obligations were not satisfied.
Defendant established entitlement to limited relief on preserved claims. The order was reversed and remitted for further proceedings.
The People's appellate arguments were rejected under the governing standards. The order was affirmed.
Any trial error was harmless under overwhelming-evidence review. Fair-trial integrity remained intact.

Defense counsel properly preserved his objection by raising the issue to the trial court when given the opportunity to make a record before jury selection. The order was reversed and a new trial ordered, in a memorandum.
Limited courtroom closures did not violate the public-trial right, but one case required a new trial due to an erroneous agency-defense jury charge.
Potential PRS violations constitute collateral plea consequences. Plea allocution need not enumerate collateral consequences.
Effective-assistance review is circumstance specific under meaningful-representation doctrine. Counsel performance failed the governing standard in this record context.
Preserved claims warranted partial corrective relief but not wholesale reversal. Liability determination sustained under controlling standards.
Buford individual juror inquiry was not required on these facts. Circumstances did not implicate the rationale for enhanced voir dire.
Superior court information held facially sufficient. Jurisdictional defect not established on the accusatory instrument.
Defendant was entitled to coram nobis relief based on ineffective appellate representation. The prior affirmance was vacated and the case remitted to the Appellate Division.
Contested ruling satisfied the applicable constitutional and statutory standard. No preserved basis for further relief.
Technical noncompliance with O'Rama/CPL 310.30 did not create mode-of-proceedings error. Preservation limits applied.
A defendant's absence alone does not waive the right to effective assistance of counsel. On this record, counsel's nonparticipation required reversal.
Entry of counsel did not, by itself, establish voluntariness of subsequent statements. Voluntariness required independent proof under Miranda and due-process principles.
Conflict-of-interest challenge did not establish an adverse effect on the defense. New-trial relief was unwarranted under governing conflict doctrine.
The trial court erred in prohibiting defendant from making a "missing witness" argument, but that the error was harmless. Harmless-error principles foreclosed relief.
Substitution of a trial judge was permissible under Judiciary Law § 21 constraints. Statutory violation and mistrial entitlement were not established.
CPL 250.10 notice requirement applied to the defense proof at issue. Psychiatric-evidence disclosure obligations were triggered by the proposed mental-condition evidence.
Defendant's sufficiency challenge was unpreserved, and the remaining claims lacked merit. The order was affirmed.
The People did not meet their burden to prove a valid inventory search under standardized procedures. Suppression relief was required.
Evidence was legally sufficient for depraved-indifference murder and first-degree manslaughter. Intent and recklessness elements were supported by the trial proof.
When a motion to withdraw a plea is patently insufficient on its face, a court may simply deny the motion without making any inquiry.
We are unable to determine that this conclusion was error as a matter of law. The order was affirmed, in a memorandum.
The order of the Appellate Division should be reversed and the case remitted to that Court for further proceedings in accordance with this memorandum.
Record supported attenuation from any antecedent illegality. Suppression denial sustained under attenuation doctrine.
Cross-examination on underlying facts of a conviction pending direct appeal was improper. Impeachment use deferred until appeal exhaustion.
Defendant failed to establish standing to challenge the search. Suppression was properly denied.
Attorney General claims against former corporate officers were legally cognizable on the pleaded theory. Record supported continuation of enforcement claims under applicable statutes.
Unpreserved claims of evidentiary error and prosecutorial misconduct did not warrant reversal. Ineffective-assistance claims were also rejected.
Imposition of mandatory postrelease supervision at resentencing did not violate the federal Double Jeopardy Clause in these circumstances.
For an eligible youth, the sentencing court had to make an express youthful-offender determination under CPL 720.20.
Warrant application and affidavit were insufficient, standing alone, to establish probable cause. Limited corrective relief was required.
Notice claim under Correction Law § 168-n was unpreserved. Preservation default barred appellate relief.
Whether defendant consented to the search was a mixed question of law and fact, and record support for consent foreclosed further review.
Failure to object when correction was possible rendered the claim unpreserved. No reviewable error remained.
A failure to exercise a peremptory challenge against a juror who was a longtime friend of the prosecuting attorney did not amount to ineffective assistance of counsel. The order was affirmed.
Challenges to the trial rulings lacked merit under governing standards. No reversible legal error established.
The challenged background evidence was properly admitted with limiting instructions. The trial court did not abuse its discretion.
Lower courts misfocused on inconsistency between trial testimony and pretrial statement. Correct legal framework required different treatment of the challenged proof.
The claim fell within the narrow preservation exception for readily apparent illegal sentences. Appellate review was therefore available.
Suppression claim did not satisfy the standard for exclusionary relief. New-trial request therefore failed.
The evidence was insufficient to allow a reasonable juror to harbor a doubt concerning the element of intent on the basis of intoxication. The order was affirmed, in a memorandum.
Recusal was discretionary absent statutory disqualification under Judiciary Law § 14. The order was affirmed.
The principal witnesses against him were accomplices, and their testimony required corroboration under CPL 60.22. Statutory corroboration requirements controlled evidentiary sufficiency.
In this case, the Appellate Division erroneously failed to assign counsel to represent defendant before dismissing his first-tier appeal as of right based on his failure to timely perfect it.
Statutory prerequisites were satisfied under the interpretation adopted by the lower courts. No legal error requiring correction.
Defendant is entitled to relief. The order was modified.
Harmless-error doctrine generally cannot salvage a guilty plea entered after erroneous suppression denial. Suppression error tainted the plea decision.
Weapon-possession offenses were complete before later criminal conduct. Consecutive sentences were therefore legally permissible.
The original conviction remained valid; resentencing relief was limited to adding mandatory postrelease supervision.
Failure to advise of potential deportation consequences did not entitle defendant to plea withdrawal under controlling precedent. Limited appellate correction was otherwise warranted.
Constitutional right asserted by defendant was not violated on this record. No remedy warranted under governing standards.
Home-or-business exception under Penal Law § 265.03 did not apply despite defendant's asserted theory. Weapon-possession conviction stood.
Prosecutorial delay did not rise to a due-process violation. Prompt-prosecution claim failed under prejudice-and-reasonableness analysis.
State and federal constitutional provisions guarantee effective assistance of counsel. Counsel performance satisfied meaningful-representation standards.
Inventory search of vehicle produced firearm and ammunition evidence. Search upheld under standardized-inventory principles and lawful impoundment.
The order of the Appellate Division should be affirmed. The order was affirmed, in a memorandum.
Interpretation of Penal Law § 70.30 advanced by respondents was rejected as inconsistent with statutory incentive structure. Lower-court result nevertheless sustained on this record.
After full and fair suppression hearing opportunity, People are not entitled to reopened hearing on remand. Havelka bar controlled.
Sufficiency claim preservation was resolved under Lopez exception analysis. Appellate preservation ruling was erroneous.
Defendant's claim that he completed his plea obligations and was entitled to dismissal was unpreserved and not reviewable.
Showup identification, traffic stop, and vehicle search challenges failed. Suppression standards were satisfied.
An acquittal on one count and conviction on another did not render the conviction legally insufficient based on factual inconsistency alone. The order was affirmed.
Legality of stop and search was undisputed. Reversal rested on separate legal error.
No preserved claim warranted merits relief. Statutory limits on appellate jurisdiction required dismissal.

Collateral estoppel was not constitutionally compelled because prior acquittal did not resolve an ultimate fact in the present prosecution. Federal due-process and double-jeopardy doctrine permitted use of the challenged proof.
The accusatory instrument for attempted seventh-degree possession was facially sufficient, including the knowledge element. The order was affirmed.
Court failed to advise that determinate sentence required mandatory PRS under Penal Law § 70.45. Defect did not warrant plea vacatur on this record.
Resentencing yielded a disposition more favorable than the original plea bargain. Plea-withdrawal remedy not required where bargain benefit was not diminished.
Unpreserved-claim ruling by Appellate Term did not control final disposition. Reversal required under the governing preservation exception analysis.
Search warrant execution at defense counsel's office implicated attorney-client and trial-fairness protections. Limited corrective relief was required.
Refusal to permit recollection refreshment with prior statement was error. Error required a new trial.
Error was not harmless because proof of guilt was not overwhelming. New trial required.
Claim was unpreserved and alternatively meritless. Preservation default independently supported affirmance.
